rewritten_text:
Noon had long gone by when he woke. His valet had several times stolen on tiptoe into the chamber to discover whether he was moving, wondering why his young master slept so late. At last the bell rang, and Victor entered quietly, bearing tea and a heap of letters on a little tray of antique Sèvres china. He pulled aside the olive satin curtains, lined with gleaming blue, which covered the three lofty windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he observed with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked sleepily.

“One hour and a quarter, Monsieur.”

So late! He raised himself, took a little tea, and looked through his correspondence. There was a letter from Lord Henry, delivered by hand that morning. After a moment’s hesitation he laid it aside. He opened the rest without interest. They offered the customary assortment of cards, dinner invitations, admission to private views, charity concert programmes, and similar things showered every morning during the season upon fashionable young gentlemen. There was a considerable bill for a Louis-Quinze dressing-table set of chased silver, which he had not yet dared forward to his guardians. They were exceedingly old-fashioned, and failed to understand that in our age superfluous things constitute our sole necessities. There were also several exquisitely polite notes from money-lenders in Jermyn Street, proposing to supply any amount at an instant’s notice on the most moderate terms.

Some ten minutes later he rose, put on an ornate dressing gown of cashmere embroidered in silk, and entered the bathroom with its onyx pavement. After his prolonged slumber, the cool water revived him. Everything he had endured seemed forgotten. Once or twice he had a vague impression of having shared in some extraordinary tragedy, but it possessed a dream’s unreality.

When dressed, he made his way to the library, where a light French breakfast awaited him on a small circular table beside the open window. The day was lovely. Spices seemed to fill the warm air. A bee entered and hummed about the bowl patterned with blue dragons, which stood before him full of sulphur-yellow roses. He was entirely happy.

All at once he noticed the screen he had set before the portrait, and gave a start.

“Monsieur finds it too cold?” inquired the valet, placing an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian moved his head in denial. “I am not cold,” he said softly.

The doctor was elderly, and when I got him out of bed he looked like a very nice, kind old man. I told him my brother and I had been hunting on Spanish Island the afternoon before, and had camped on a section of raft we found. Around midnight my brother must have kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to come over and treat it without telling anyone or letting people find out, since we planned to get home that evening and surprise the family.

“Who’s your family?” he asked.

“The Phelpses, down there.”

“Oh,” he said. After a moment he asked:

“How did you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I said, “and it shot him.”

“An unusual dream,” he said.

He lit his lantern, picked up his saddlebags, and we set off. But he didn’t like the look of the canoe when he saw it. He said it was large enough for one person, but didn’t seem very safe for two. I said:

“You don’t need to worry, sir. It carried all three of us easily enough.”

“Which three?”

“Me and Sid, and—and—and the guns. That’s what I meant.”

“Oh,” he said.

But he set a foot on the side and rocked it, then shook his head and said he thought he’d find a bigger one. All the others were locked and chained, though, so he took my canoe. He told me to wait until he returned, or keep looking for another, or perhaps go home and get everyone ready for the surprise if I liked. I said I didn’t want to. I explained exactly where to find the raft, and off he went.

Pretty soon something occurred to me. Suppose he couldn’t fix that leg in a flash, as people say? Suppose he needed three or four days? What would we do—hang around until he gave the secret away? No, sir. I knew what I’d do. I would wait, and if he came back saying he needed to return, I would get there too, even if I had to swim. We would tie him up, keep him with us, and head downriver. Once Tom no longer needed him, we would pay him what the treatment was worth, or everything we had, and let him go ashore.

Then I crawled into a stack of lumber for some sleep. When I woke, the sun was high overhead! I rushed out and ran to the doctor’s house, where they said he had left sometime during the night and still hadn’t returned.

I walked quickly, and we soon reached my college. Then a thought struck me that made me shudder: the creature I had left in my rooms might still be there, alive and moving about. I dreaded seeing the monster, but dreaded even more the possibility that Henry would see him. I begged Henry to wait a few minutes at the foot of the stairs and hurried up to my room. My hand had already reached the door lock when I stopped to collect myself. I paused, trembling with cold fear. Then I flung the door open, like a child who expects a ghost to be waiting on the other side. Nothing appeared. I stepped inside in terror. The room was empty, and my bedroom, too, was free of its hideous visitor. I could scarcely believe I had been so lucky. Once I was certain my enemy had truly escaped, I clapped my hands with delight and ran downstairs to Clerval.

We went up to my room together, and soon the servant brought breakfast, but I could not control myself. Joy was only part of what I felt. My skin tingled with an overwhelming sensitivity, and my heart raced. I could not stay still for even an instant. I leaped over chairs, clapped, and laughed out loud. At first Clerval thought my unusually high spirits came from my happiness at seeing him. But as he watched more closely, he noticed an inexplicable wildness in my eyes. My loud, uncontrolled laughter, with no real feeling behind it, shocked and frightened him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “for God’s sake, what is wrong? Please don’t laugh like that. You look so ill! What has brought this on?”

“Don’t ask me!” I cried, covering my eyes, because I thought I saw the dreaded figure slip into the room. “He can tell you. Oh, save me! Save me!” I imagined the monster had grabbed me. I struggled violently, then collapsed in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What could he have felt? A reunion he had awaited with such joy had taken this strange and bitter turn. But I did not see his grief. I lay unconscious, and a very long time passed before my senses returned.

This marked the beginning of a nervous fever that kept me confined for several months. Henry alone nursed me throughout that time. I later learned that he concealed how serious my illness was to spare my family the distress. He knew that my father was too old to manage such a long journey and that news of my sickness would make Elizabeth miserable.
